intro:
**The Crowning Victory and the Prophet's Farewell**

An-Naṣr, "The Divine Support" or "The Victory"—also known universally as *Sūrat al-Tawdīʿ* (The Chapter of Farewell)—is the one-hundred-and-tenth chapter of the Qur'an, comprising 3 verses. Chronologically, it holds a deeply emotional, monumental status in Islamic history: it was the *very last complete sūrah of the Qur'an ever revealed* to the Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ, descending at Mina during the Farewell Pilgrimage (*Ḥajjat al-Wadāʿ*) in the 10th year of the Hijrah, merely months before the Messenger's passing. It takes its name from verse 1: *“When the victory of Allah has come and the conquest, and you see the people entering into the religion of Allah in multitudes...”* (110:1–2). In three sublime, luminous verses, Sūrah an-Naṣr announces the triumphant culmination of the prophetic mission: the conquest of Makkah, the peaceful submission of the Arabian tribes, and commands the Prophet to conclude his earthly life with glorification, praise, and seeking divine forgiveness (*fa-sabbiḥ bi-ḥamdi Rabbika wa-staghfirh*).

**The Tears of Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb**

In Islamic history, Sūrah an-Naṣr is commemorated by an extraordinary assembly recorded in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī (4294). The Caliph ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb was accustomed to seating the youthful ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās among the elder veterans of Badr. Some elders whispered among themselves: *“Why does ʿUmar seat this young boy with us when we have sons his age?”* To show Ibn ʿAbbās's peerless insight, ʿUmar gathered the Badr veterans and asked them: *“What do you say concerning the statement of Allah: 'When the victory of Allah has come and the conquest'?”* The elders replied: *“We are commanded to praise Allah and seek His forgiveness when He grants us victory and conquests.”* ʿUmar then turned to Ibn ʿAbbās: *“Do you say the same, O Ibn ʿAbbās?”* The young scholar replied: *“No! It is the announcement of the impending death of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ! Allah notified him that his earthly mission was complete: 'When the victory of Allah has come and the conquest of Makkah—that is the sign of your term's end; so glorify the praise of your Lord and seek His forgiveness; indeed, He is ever Accepting of repentance!'”* ʿUmar said: *“I know nothing of it except what you have said!”*

verses.1:
> When Allah’s ˹ultimate˺ help comes and the victory ˹over Mecca is achieved˺

**Help and Opening Are Two Different Gifts**

Two nouns hold the verse up, and they are not synonyms. *Naṣr* is help given inside a struggle — support arriving when one side cannot win alone, which is why the Qur'an makes it God's to give rather than a property of armies: *“If Allah helps you, none can defeat you. But if He denies you help, then who else can help you?”* (3:160). *Fatḥ* is an opening. Its root *f-t-ḥ* means to open what was shut, and from that base it names both the opening of a city's gates and the opening of a case — a verdict delivered between parties who have argued too long. A city that resisted is opened; a dispute is settled.

**Mecca Fell in Ramadan of the Eighth Year**

The bracketed words in the translation name the event most commentators mean: the conquest of Mecca. It took place in Ramadan 8 AH, which falls in January 630 CE. The Prophet ﷺ marched with roughly ten thousand men, the largest force ever to leave Medina, and the city came over with almost no fighting; the general amnesty granted afterwards is what made the second verse of this sūrah possible. Quraysh had held out for eight years after the Hijrah, and their resistance had been the last public argument against the message.

Two readings compete with this one. Some take the *fatḥ* to be the Treaty of Ḥudaybiyyah of 6 AH (628 CE), because the Qur'an itself calls that treaty *“a clear triumph ˹O Prophet˺”* (48:1) and because the truce that followed produced conversions on a scale Mecca had never seen. Others read the verse as pointing to the conquests after the Prophet's death, when Islam crossed the borders of Arabia. The first has the stronger claim.

Ibn Kathir notes that the early commentators held a single unanimous position regarding the identity of the opening (*al-Fatḥ*): it is specifically the conquest of Makkah. Across the Arabian peninsula, the various tribes had held back from accepting Islam, closely watching how the struggle between the Prophet ﷺ and his own people would conclude. They said among themselves: *“Leave him and his people alone; if he is victorious over them, then he is a true prophet.”* Al-Bukhārī recorded in his Ṣaḥīḥ from ʿAmr ibn Salamah that when Makkah fell without prolonged resistance, the Arab delegations rushed from every region to profess their faith before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Within two years of that decisive victory, the entire Arabian peninsula was laden with faith, and no tribe remained without accepting Islam.

**The Oldest Reading of This Verse Was That It Announced a Death**

One day ʿUmar asked the gathering what they made of *“When comes the Help of Allah and the Conquest.”* Some answered that believers are commanded to praise God and seek His forgiveness when help and conquest reach them; others said nothing at all. Turning to Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿUmar was told that this is the appointed term of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, made known to him: the help and the conquest are the sign of it, and the praise and the seeking of forgiveness are what he is to do with the time remaining. ʿUmar's answer is recorded in the same report — he knew nothing about the verse beyond what this young man had said. It stands in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 4970, from Ibn ʿAbbās through Saʿīd ibn Jubayr.

So the first generation read the condition as a notice of departure. The Qur'an states the principle elsewhere without softening it: *“We have not granted immortality to any human before you ˹O Prophet˺: so if you die, will they live forever?”* (21:34).

**The Last Complete Chapter, With a Few Verses After It**

Most exegetes put this sūrah at the end of the revelation, as the last chapter given whole. Individual verses came later — among them 2:281 — *“Be mindful of the Day when you will ˹all˺ be returned to Allah, then every soul will be paid in full for what it has done, and none will be wronged”*, 4:176 — *“They ask you ˹for a ruling, O Prophet˺.”* and 9:128 — *“There certainly has come to you a messenger from among yourselves. He is concerned by your suffering, anxious for your well-being, and gracious and merciful to the believers”*, and, on the strongest account, 5:3 — *“Forbidden to you are carrion, blood, and swine; what is slaughtered in the name of any other than Allah; what is killed by strangling, beating, a fall, or by being gored to death; what is partly eaten by a predator unless you slaughter it; and what is sacrificed on altars.”* at the Farewell Pilgrimage. The disagreement concerns the setting rather than the rank. Some place the revelation at Minā on the tenth of Dhū l-Ḥijjah during that pilgrimage, a day after 5:3 — *“Forbidden to you are carrion, blood, and swine; what is slaughtered in the name of any other than Allah; what is killed by strangling, beating, a fall, or by being gored to death; what is partly eaten by a predator unless you slaughter it; and what is sacrificed on altars.”*; others place it immediately before 5:3 — *“Forbidden to you are carrion, blood, and swine; what is slaughtered in the name of any other than Allah; what is killed by strangling, beating, a fall, or by being gored to death; what is partly eaten by a predator unless you slaughter it; and what is sacrificed on altars.”*; others hold that it came in Medina after the Prophet ﷺ had returned home. A minority dates it to right after Ḥudaybiyyah in 6 AH, and al-Wāḥidī sets it at the departure for Ḥunayn in 8 AH, roughly two years before the end.

Arabic regularly puts a future event in the perfect when its realization is so certain that the language treats it as finished, and the Qur'an uses that device wherever certainty is the point: *“The command of Allah is at hand, so do not hasten it.”* (16:1).

Contrast that with the chapter two places on in the codex, where the Qur'an names a living opponent in its very first line (111:1 — *“May the hands of Abu Lahab perish, and he ˹himself˺ perish”*).

The singular status of this chapter as the final complete revelation is reinforced by early transmission. An-Nasāʾī recorded from ʿUbaydullāh ibn ʿAbdillāh ibn ʿUtbah that Ibn ʿAbbās asked him: “Do you know the last sūrah of the Qur'an that was revealed as a whole?” When Ibn ʿUtbah recited this chapter, Ibn ʿAbbās confirmed that he had spoken the truth. Imām Aḥmad recorded from Ibn ʿAbbās that upon its revelation, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ declared: “My death has been announced to me,” and he passed away within that very year. Classical scholars also noted that this chapter was reckoned in virtue as equal to one-fourth of the Qur'an, placed alongside Sūrat az-Zalzalah.
verses.2:
> and you ˹O Prophet˺ see the people embracing Allah’s Way in crowds

**A Sign That Has to Be Seen With the Eyes**

The second condition is perceptual. *Raʾayta* — you saw — is a verb of sight, and the verse puts the Prophet ﷺ in the position of a witness rather than of someone receiving information. God could have said simply that the people have entered. Instead the sentence waits for the sight of it: when you *see* them entering.

That verb has a wider use in Arabic. *Raʾā* can mean to know or to judge, as when a speaker says "I see that this is so," and some commentators read it that way here, taking the verse to describe realization rather than observation. The dispute matters less than it looks, because both readings keep the weight on evidence. What the sūrah waits for is a state of affairs that can be checked in the world: crowds, visible, arriving. Faith at this scale leaves a social trace — delegations on the road, oaths taken in public, whole districts changing allegiance — and the verse treats the trace as the sign.

**Afwājā Is the Qur'an's Word for a Procession**

The Qur'an reserves this word for processions of consequence. The damned are driven to Hell *“in ˹successive˺ groups”* (39:71), and the righteous are led to Paradise under the same term (39:73 — *“And those who were mindful of their Lord will be led to Paradise in ˹successive˺ groups.”*); when the Trumpet is blown, humanity *“will ˹all˺ come forth in crowds”* (78:18). Each time *afwāj* describes a multitude moving toward a destination it cannot leave, company after company. Used here, the word gives the spread of Islam the shape of a Last-Day procession: not scattered conversions but an ordered arrival.

While the verse commemorates the sweeping historic arrival of the Arabian tribes embracing the faith in multitudes, the early community also recorded a prophetic warning concerning the fragility of later generations. Imām Aḥmad recorded from Abū ʿAmmār that a neighbor of Jābir ibn ʿAbdillāh returned from a journey and went to greet Jābir. As they spoke of the emerging divisions, dissension, and innovations appearing among the people, Jābir began to weep and said: “I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: ‘Verily, the people entered into the religion of Allah in crowds, and they will also leave it in crowds.’” The preservation of this report alongside the verse emphasizes that mass entry is a gift whose preservation requires continual adherence, steadfastness, and collective unity.

**Entering God's Way, Not Joining a Man's Party**

The same phrase carries the Qur'an's own definition: *“Certainly, Allah's only Way is Islam.”* (3:19). And this claim has to be held together with another Madinan verse, which states that faith cannot be forced: *“Let there be no compulsion in religion, for the truth stands out clearly from falsehood.”* (2:256). The two are reconciled by the amnesty at Mecca. The city was taken, the population was pardoned, and the entry that followed was chosen by people who had been given the option of remaining exactly as they were. That is why the Qur'an can describe mass conversion without embarrassment: the crowd arrived after the sword had been sheathed, not because of it.

**The Promise Fulfilled in Truth**

Two earlier revelations described this scene before it happened, and the verse reads as their discharge. During the truce year the Prophet ﷺ had been shown in a dream that he would enter the Sacred Mosque; the Qur'an confirmed the dream and explained the delay: *“Indeed, Allah will fulfil His Messenger's vision in all truth: Allah willing, you will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, in security... He knew what you did not know, so He first granted you the triumph at hand.”* (48:27). What the sūrah of Victory announced as coming, this sūrah reports as arrived.

The other promise was broader, and it carried a condition: *“Allah has promised those of you who believe and do good that He will certainly make them successors in the land, as He did with those before them. And will surely establish for them their faith which He has chosen for them; and will indeed change their fear into security—˹provided that˺ they worship Me, associating nothing with Me.”* (24:55). The condition and the crowds meet in the verse that follows.
verses.3:
> then glorify the praises of your Lord and seek His forgiveness, for certainly He is ever Accepting of Repentance

**Glorify With Praise: Two Acts in a Single Phrase**

*Sabbiḥ bi-ḥamd rabbika* joins two things that are often separated. *Tasbīḥ* is to declare God beyond what is said of Him — the removal of every deficiency and every likeness; *ḥamd* is praise for what He is and what He has done. Joined by the preposition *bi-*, they become one act: glorify Him *with* praise, so that the removal of imperfection does not slide into a God who is merely distant, and the praise does not slide into a God who is merely generous.

The same formula recurs at turning points in the revelation: *“So glorify the praises of your Lord and be one of those who ˹always˺ pray”* (15:98); *“So be patient ˹O Prophet˺, ˹for˺ Allah's promise is certainly true. Seek forgiveness for your shortcomings. And glorify the praises of your Lord morning and evening.”* (40:55); and again at 20:130 — *“So be patient ˹O Prophet˺ with what they say.”* and 50:39 — *“So be patient ˹O Prophet˺ with what they say. And glorify the praises of your Lord before sunrise and before sunset”*. In each case glorification is paired with patience or with prayer, and in 40:55 — *“So be patient ˹O Prophet˺, ˹for˺ Allah’s promise is certainly true. Seek forgiveness for your shortcomings. And glorify the praises of your Lord morning and evening”* with the request for forgiveness exactly as here.

The Prophet ﷺ put the pairing into his own prayer. ʿĀʾishah reported that he often said while bowing and prostrating: "Glory be to You, O Allah, our Lord, and praise be to You; O Allah, forgive me" — and she added that he was putting the Qur'an into practice. The report is in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 484. The formula she quotes contains all three elements of this verse in a single breath.

The direct lived implementation of this command is preserved in an authentic report recorded by both Imām Aḥmad and Muslim from Masrūq, from ʿĀʾishah. She related that toward the end of his life, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ frequently repeated: “Glory be to Allah and His is the praise; I seek Allah’s forgiveness and repent to Him.” When she inquired why he had adopted this supplication so constantly, the Prophet ﷺ explained: “My Lord informed me that I would see a sign in my community, and He commanded me that when I see it, I should glorify His praises and seek His forgiveness, for He is ever Accepting of repentance — and I have indeed seen it.” He then recited the entirety of this sūrah, showing that the verse functioned as both a divine foretelling and a daily devotional practice.

**Asking Forgiveness at the Top of Success**

The first is that a victory of this size carries real liabilities. The third is simply the Prophet's own habit, which the Qur'an confirms rather than introduces. He said: "By Allah, I ask Allah's forgiveness and turn to Him more than seventy times a day" — Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 6307, from Abū Hurayrah.

Elsewhere the same pairing is addressed to him directly with the community included: *“And seek forgiveness for your shortcomings and for ˹the sins of˺ the believing men and women.”* (47:19).

Ibn Kathir notes that commanding forgiveness at the pinnacle of triumph reflects an established rhythm across sacred acts in the Qur'an. Exalted deeds of devotion routinely conclude with *istighfār*: the daily prescribed prayers finish with seeking forgiveness three times; the rites of pilgrimage terminate with the command to seek divine pardon after descending from the plain of ʿArafāt (2:199 — *“And seek Allah’s forgiveness”*); and the devout vigil during the late night is sealed with prayer for pardon before the break of dawn (51:18 — *“and pray for forgiveness before dawn”*). Concluding the prophetic conveyance itself with praise and repentance teaches that the greatest human achievement still bows before divine perfection, leaving the servant with humility rather than self-praise.

**Tawwāb: The Name That Turns First**

The Qur'an exploits that reciprocity. Adam receives words of prayer and is forgiven: *“Then Adam was inspired with words ˹of prayer˺ by his Lord, so He accepted his repentance. Surely He is the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful.”* (2:37). The three who stayed behind from Tabūk are described in the longest such sentence in the Book: *“They knew there was no refuge from Allah except in Him. Then He turned to them in mercy so that they might repent.”* (9:118) — His turning comes first, and their turning is its result. That is the religious content of the name in this verse. A man at the height of success is told to ask forgiveness, and the reason he can ask is that the asking has already been met. *Tawwāb* is not a promise that God will be persuaded; it is a statement that He begins.

**Endings Are Described the Same Way Throughout the Book**

Two other verses belong with this one, and reading them together shows the Qur'an's consistent way of handling an ending. The first prepares the community for a death it did not want: *“Muḥammad is no more than a messenger; other messengers have gone before him. If he were to die or to be killed, would you regress into disbelief?”* (3:144) — revealed at Uḥud, years before the conquest, and proved necessary on the day he died, when some refused to believe it.

The second is the verse most often reported as the last revealed of all: *“Be mindful of the Day when you will ˹all˺ be returned to Allah, then every soul will be paid in full for what it has done, and none will be wronged.”* (2:281). Both are addresses about return — the messenger's return to his Lord, and every soul's return to be paid. The instruction to glorify and seek forgiveness sits between them. It is what a person does with the interval, and this sūrah measures the interval in months.
